newsitem.title: ITALY: Di Pietro resignation shocks Italian government.
newsitem.headline: Di Pietro resignation shocks Italian government.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi faced calls for his resignation as his centre-left government grappled with the unwelcome shock of national hero Antonio Di Pietro quitting as public works minister.
Di Pietro became a people's hero as the star investigator of Milan's elite "Clean Hands" magistrates, whose bombshell corruption probes brought down Italy's political old guard.
He resigned on Thursday after coming under investigation himself for alleged malpractice while spearheading the famous "Tangentopoli" (Bribesville) probes.

If confirmed, the resignation would be the first in Prodi's cabinet and would come at a delicate time for the government, which is trying to push its controversial 1997 budget package through parliament amid determined centre-right opposition.
Some in the opposition, which has bitterly boycotted debate on the budget in parliament's lower house, said the resignation would affect the stability of the six-month-old government.
"Obviously the Prodi government, already seriously weakened by the budget wrangle, has been weakened even further," said Pierferdinando Casini, head of the small Christian Democratic Centre party.
"At this point Prodi himself must resign to give a minimum of dignity to this indecent episode," added Giulio Maceratini, head of the hard-right National Alliance party in the senate.
But the government rushed to limit the potential damage, saying Di Pietro's move would not hurt its stability.
"I don't believe it will have an impact on the executive but it will affect the public works ministry, which had been functioning very well," deputy premier Walter Veltroni said.
Prodi, in a speech to parliament, urged Di Pietro to change his mind "and continue to give his precious contribution to the government". But the appeal appeared to be rejected.

His spokeswoman, Sonia Mancini, said Di Pietro's decision was "absolutely irrevocable" and while a flurry of centre-left leaders also urged him to stay on, a long-time friend of his said he had made up his mind.
"Di Pietro is stubborn and I don't think he will go back on his decision," parliamentarian Elio Veltri told reporters.
"He will go back to teaching at university, which he likes better than being a minister," Veltri added.
Di Pietro, in a letter to Prodi on Thursday, said he was going because he was the victim of a political "pigeon shoot".

The angry move, which followed confirmation from his lawyer that he was under preliminary investigation by magistrates in the northern town of Brescia, was not the first time Di Pietro had tendered a high-profile resignation.

He quit as a magistrate in December 1994 shortly after the Milan team placed then conservative premier Silvio Berlusconi under investigation for alleged bribery. But he has never fully explained why he resigned.
Newspapers on Thursday said Di Pietro was being probed over alleged irregularities in the way he conducted his inquiries.

"For years I have been subjected to probes and enquiries of all kinds, legal and illegal, and always unjustly," Di Pietro, who was previously probed by Brescia magistrates but cleared of all charges, wrote in his resignation letter.

"Even so, the pigeon shoot goes on because they are trying to make me pay at any cost for the only thing they can pin on me, and of which I'm proud, and that is that I wanted to do my duty," he wrote.
